author: Nickolaus Kelly
text:
The first hiring mistake in an AI CoE is hiring a data scientist.

Not because data scientists don’t matter. They do.

But if you hire them first, everything downstream of the model becomes someone else’s problem.

And then it becomes nobody’s problem.

This week’s issue is about the seven roles that actually matter when building an AI Center of Excellence, based on scaling a 35+ person CoE at IBM and standing up EpositBox from zero.

The order matters:

Head of Governance 
Someone has to own the responsible AI framework, tiering rubric, and audit posture before the first regulator question arrives.

Lead architect
 Without architecture patterns, every use case becomes a custom build.
Adoption / enablement lead

Most CoEs stall because training, ambassadors, and change management are treated like side work.

Senior ML / applied AI engineer
 Now you hire the model person, once the operating frame exists.

AI program manager
Someone has to own intake, routing, stage gates, and cross-functional cadence.

Evaluation engineer
Before Tier 2 use cases hit production, evaluation and drift detection need a clear owner.

Executive narrative lead
The board deck, business case, and ROI story cannot be an afterthought.
I also cover the roles I’d push back on in the first 18 months, including AI evangelists with no delivery accountability, dedicated prompt engineers, and chief AI officers without budget or authority.

text:
SKILLS DRIFT: I've got a slightly contrary take on the cysec skills gap issue. We know it requires more budget and time to train up. But #cybersecurity isn’t suffering because people lack expertise. It’s more because the definition of expertise keeps mutating faster than orgs can update their job architecture. 

AI governance roles didn’t exist four years ago. AI/ML security specialists weren’t standard hires. Regulatory frameworks like NIS2, DORA, and DoD 8140 are rewriting what “qualified” even means. The workforce isn’t short on talent as much as it’s short on alignment. In other words, teams are structured around legacy assumptions.

The real bottleneck I see is that companies are still hiring for yesterday’s threat model while operating inside today’s regulatory model and defending against tomorrow’s AI‑accelerated threat model. That "temporal mismatch" creates a workforce problem no amount of budget can solve.

Titles that once made sense (analyst, engineer, architect) now hide wildly different responsibilities depending on the organization. AI governance, ML security, exposure management, cloud‑native detection, etc. 

These are not “specializations.” They’re entirely new disciplines. Yet most companies still write job descriptions as if the environment were frozen in 2019. But you may disagree, let me know.

author: Amit Goel, open to work
text:
Is the growth of Global Capability Centers (GCCs) slowing down in Bengaluru? 

Let's start with the facts: Bengaluru remains a leader with over 875 GCCs, accounting for approximately 27-36% of the national base, and nearly 50% of India's AI/ML talent. The city hosts 27% of all Indian GCCs and 37% of GCC talent. However, Hyderabad and Pune are experiencing faster growth from a smaller base, attracting new openings for various reasons. 

In the first two months of 2026 alone, three major GCCs launched in Hyderabad, solidifying its position as India's fastest-growing GCC destination. While Bengaluru excels in expansions and AI-specific mandates, Hyderabad is capturing a significant share of new logos. 

Why are companies choosing Hyderabad and Pune over Bengaluru? 
- **Cost**: Pune offers 20-30% lower costs than Bengaluru, with attrition around 14%. A 100-engineer center in Pune is significantly cheaper annually than in Bengaluru. 
- **Attrition**: Bengaluru's attrition often exceeds 20% for competitive engineering roles, with aggressive counter-offers. In contrast, Bengaluru and Hyderabad's attrition ranges from 16-18%, prompting GCCs to establish satellite locations. 
- **Infrastructure/Talent Saturation**: Metro hubs are becoming saturated, leading to tighter competition in real estate, commuting, and hiring pools in Bengaluru. 
- **Policy Push**: Hyderabad benefits from a policy-driven, digital-first ecosystem with strong BFSI presence, supported by initiatives like the Telangana AI Mission and AI City, providing a balanced cost-to-capability advantage. 
- **Domain Fit**: Pune has evolved into a hub for enterprise services and shared operations, while Hyderabad excels in life sciences and biotech due to its Genome Valley ecosystem. 

The trend is shifting towards a hub-and-spoke model, where leadership remains in Bengaluru or Hyderabad, engineering scales in Pune or Chennai, and cost-efficient back-office work is moved to tier-2 cities. This indicates that Bengaluru is not losing its significance but rather narrowing its role to leadership and AI-core functions. 

Looking ahead, Bengaluru will likely maintain its #1 position but may see its share soften. It will continue to dominate in AI/ML, deep-tech, and Fortune 500 engineering HQs. The market is not moving away from Bengaluru; instead, it is transitioning to a model where Bengaluru anchors leadership and AI-core, while execution scales disperse to Pune, Hyderabad, Chennai, and tier-2 cities. 

To win GCC leadership by 2030, companies must architect their strategies across cities, maintaining leadership in Bengaluru, scaling in Pune or Hyderabad, and ensuring cost efficiency in tier-2 locations.

author: Dhruvil K.
text:
I keep seeing the same headline : “AI is replacing data scientists.”

But I don’t really buy that as the main storyline.

What I’m noticing while I’m making my move into data science and AI engineering feels a bit messier than that. Like, titles change , but the heartbeat underneath is still there.

The job title is shifting, not really vanishing.

This year, “AI Engineer” looks like it has overtaken a lot of the older Data Analyst and Data Scientist listings. And then there’s the newer stuff popping up constantly: GenAI Engineer, Agentic AI Engineer. you see it everywhere. Still , the core work feels kind of familiar: understanding data, building models, and knowing when to trust them or when not to.

Agentic AI is the biggest shift I’m tracking.

The agent market is projected to grow from about $5B in 2024 to more than $47B by 2030. Most companies that are just “experimenting” with agents today are already pushing them toward production. So the value isn’t only in constructing a model anymore. It’s in designing systems that can reason, use tools, and make decisions with actual business context, not just a demo vibe.

LLM experience is basically table stakes now.

It shows up in around 1 in 5 AI job postings, usually alongside things like RAG , prompt engineering, and vector databases. If you’re entering this field now, that part is the baseline. It’s not the thing that makes you stand out.

So what’s the real differentiator, then?

Judgment.

As AI systems do more of the routine analysis, companies seem to be paying for the person who can ask the right question, spot the wrong answer before it becomes a disaster, and connect the output back to a business decision. That’s not really a course thing. It’s something you bring from wherever you came from.

I’m switching into data science and AI engineering as a career changer, and honestly, it’s starting to feel like a legit advantage instead of a gap. I’m not only learning how to build models. I’m learning how to build them for problems I actually understand from the ground up.

The AI conversation is no longer about the future. It's showing up in GDP.

Recently I came across a data point, that suggests that without AI infrastructure investments, GPUs, data centers, networking, storage, and power - the U.S. economy would have looked dramatically different. In Q1 2026, annualized GDP growth was 2.0%, but AI-related investments accounted for an estimated 1.34 percentage points of that growth. Strip those investments away, and growth would have been close to flat.

Think about that for a second.

This isn't just another technology cycle anymore. AI infrastructure is becoming economic infrastructure.

But here's what caught my attention from a hiring perspective. Every wave of infrastructure spending creates an entirely new talent economy. Cloud computing created demand for cloud architects. Cybersecurity created an entirely new security workforce. Digital transformation fueled hiring across software, product, and data.

AI is doing the same, but at a much larger scale.
We're already seeing demand accelerate for:
• AI Engineers & Applied Scientists
• Data Engineers & ML Engineers
• Infrastructure & Platform Engineers

And this is just the first-order effect. The second-order impact will be even larger as every industry, from healthcare and manufacturing to financial services and retail, retools around AI-first workflows.

For hiring leaders, the question is no longer "Should we invest in AI talent?"
It's "Can we compete if we don't?" The companies that build strong AI talent pipelines today will likely be the ones defining their industries over the next decade.

Singapore’s Hiring & Labor Market Trends: What You Need to Know
Singapore’s labor market remains resilient with steady employment growth and low unemployment. However, with global economic uncertainties and cost pressures, employers are adopting a more measured, selective approach to recruitment.

1. High-Demand Sectors & Roles

Artificial Intelligence & Technology: AI adoption is a top priority across industries. High demand for AI Engineers, ML Specialists, Data Scientists, and Software Developers, alongside professionals with AI governance and prompt engineering skills.

Cybersecurity & Cloud Computing: Critical need for Security Analysts and Cloud Architects to strengthen digital resilience.

Life Sciences & Healthcare: Driven by biotech and personalized medicine. Registered Nurses, Health Data Analysts, and R&D Specialists remain heavily recruited.

Green Economy & Sustainability: ESG Analysts and Sustainability Officers are increasingly vital as companies align with Singapore's green targets.
Financial Services & FinTech: Stable demand for specialized finance, risk management, compliance, and FinTech product development.

Key Employer Priorities

Skills-Based Hiring Over Degrees: Employers value practical digital fluency, adaptability, and problem-solving over traditional linear career paths.
Internal Mobility & Retention: Heavy investment in upskilling and internal development to retain existing talent amidst niche shortages.
Agile Staffing: Rise in contract and project-based roles, particularly for digital transformation and change management initiatives.

text:
Why do companies want ONE person to know Excel, Power BI, SQL, Python, MongoDB, Azure, Kafka, Snowflake, Oracle, Tableau, AWS, AND Machine Learning... for a "Data Analyst" role?
Let's be honest about what this actually is:
1. Cost-cutting disguised as a job description.
Instead of hiring a Data Analyst + Data Engineer + BI Developer + ML Engineer (4 people, 4 salaries), companies write one JD hoping to get all 4 skill sets for the price of one. It's not "high standards" — it's budget compression.
2. Pressure shifted onto the employee.
When one person is expected to do the job of a team, workload doesn't shrink — it just gets absorbed by that one person. Missed deadlines become "you should manage your time better," not "this was never a one-person job."
3. The "competitive salary" line usually isn't competitive with the ask.
If a role genuinely needs 12 tools mastered, it should pay like 3-4 specialized roles combined. It almost never does.
And here's the part that stings more in India specifically — every company talks about "work-life balance" in their careers page, their culture deck, their onboarding email... and then writes job descriptions like this. You can't ask for balance and then structure roles that require someone to be an entire data team by themselves. That's not balance, that's just unpaid overtime with a nicer PowerPoint.
I'm not against learning broadly — most analysts pick up adjacent tools over time. But there's a difference between "nice to have" and "non-negotiable requirement," and job postings keep blurring that line to justify underpaying and overloading one person.
Curious what others in the data/analytics space think — is this a hiring trend you've noticed too, or is it worse in certain industries?

author: Ben Feifke
text:
Everybody's going crazy about Forward Deployed Engineers (FDEs)... but what if they're wrong?


💡 I was interviewing a candidate last week, and he said something that stuck with me:

"The forward deployed engineer will eventually just become a customer service role."


🤔 At first I pushed back. But then I thought about the "Lindy Effect", which says: 

"The expected remaining lifetime of non-perishable things (like technologies or books) is proportional to how long it's already existed."


So, a book that's been in print for 100 years will probably be in print for another 100; a job title that's been around for 3 months... may only last another 3 months.


📊 Consider:

- "Data Scientist" has been around since ~2008. Still here, but the definition keeps shifting, and it fell dramatically out of fashion compared to ML Engineer and Data Engineer

- "Analytics Engineer" was effectively created by dbt ~7 years ago. Already feeling the pressure from AI tooling?

- "Forward Deployed Engineer" became popular... late last year?


🔮 My take: FDEs are real and valuable today. But the role might evolve faster than people expect. After all, don't forget -- it's only 2-3 years ago that the market was going crazy hiring Prompt Engineers!

- The "forward deployed" part, delivering customer success, that's timeless.

- The "engineer" part, building elegant software solutions, that's also timeless.

- 💡 The hypothesis here is that the blend of the two might not be necessary for so long.


Maybe in 5 years, an "FDE" is really just a technical account manager with great prompting skills...

I don't know, time will tell...


What do you think: are FDEs really here to stay, or are they yet another transitional role in the tech job market? 👇
